title: Breaking and Entering: Daniel Avery Returns With a Tremor
transcript:
Daniel Avery spoke with Lauren Taylor remotely, ahead of bringing his Tremor live show to Melbourne Town Hall. Broadcast on Breaking and Entering, Triple R, 28 May 2026. Edited for length and clarity.

Lauren: Daniel Avery began DJing as a teenager at a local indie club night, spanning everything from electroclash to post-punk, and began producing and DJing back in 2009 under the name Stopmakingme, collaborating with artists like Hercules and Love Affair and Metronomy, and regularly performing at the iconic Fabric club in London. He was taken under the wing of producers like Erol Alkan, and also Andrew Weatherall, whose legacy, and what he gleaned from the late, great man, Daniel speaks about in this interview. Since his debut record, Drone Logic, in 2013, Daniel has collaborated with numerous artists, including Kelly Lee Owens and Jonny Greenwood from Radiohead, and in 2020 he released a collaborative album with Alessandro Cortini from Nine Inch Nails.

He's known for his left-field electronic production, but his latest album, Tremor, sees him returning somewhat to his roots in the shoegaze bands he played in as a teenager. He's cited early guitar music like Nine Inch Nails, the Deftones and My Bloody Valentine as huge formative influences. He has Australian connections, too: HTRK are apparently one of his favourite bands of all time. So we began the interview by asking Daniel what HTRK's music means to him.

Daniel: Easily one of my favourite bands of all time. I discovered them when I'd just moved to London, so for me they really soundtracked those hazy early days in London nightlife as a youngster. I always think that if the Velvet Underground and Nico were making records now, they might sound a bit like HTRK, and I mean that as the biggest compliment. It was such a dream working with Jonnine on that track. I love her.

Lauren: You name-checked HTRK recently as one of your favourite shoegaze artists, perfect for a post-rave come-down, as well as another Australian act who are joining me on the show in a couple of weeks, Acopia. It's really great to see them doing so well on the world stage. How did you discover Acopia?

Daniel: A friend of mine, Palms Trax, a DJ, re-released their debut record and asked me to do a remix, and I just fell in love with them straight away. There's just so much great music of that variety coming out of Australia, particularly Melbourne. I don't know what you have in the water there, but something about that real broken-beauty shoegaze, with loads of pop hooks in it. I love it.

Lauren: If you're a shoegaze fan, I don't know if you've seen that Simon Reynolds has a new shoegaze book coming out.

Daniel: I have it. They sent me an early copy.

Lauren: Worth reading, I imagine. He's incredible.

Daniel: It's really good. It's a really interesting read, because he talks about how this is a book he's wanted to write for a long time, because he was right in the heart of that scene. So it's as much about being a music fan as being a music historian. It's really cool.

Lauren: Congratulations on the new record, Tremor, whose deluxe version has just come out with some new remixes. You're known for your otherworldly club bangers and your left-field production, but as a teenager you were playing in shoegaze bands and, I understand, worshipping at the altar of guitar bands like the Deftones, Nine Inch Nails and My Bloody Valentine. Do the new record and these full-band live shows feel like a return to your roots?

Daniel: They do. It feels like a sort of full-circle moment, but at the same time, I never want it to feel like a throwback or anything. The album, the music and the live shows have all the techno elements I've picked up along the way over the years. It's a real mixture of everything that has shaped me. It's interesting to me, because a few people have said, well, if this was where you began, why haven't you done it before? And I don't have a great answer, other than I just don't think I could have done it. For whatever reason, I'm feeling a certain level of freedom at the moment, and I feel as if it's taken this long to incubate the idea. And here we are.

Lauren: We mentioned Nine Inch Nails, and you've got a great record with Nine Inch Nails synth savant Alessandro Cortini, from 2020, called Illusion of Time. Was that another full-circle moment, getting to work with one of your heroes?

Daniel: Absolutely. And it's still one of my favourite things I've done. I'm so proud of it. I was actually just talking about that record with someone yesterday. By complete chance, it came out at the very beginning of lockdown, and it soundtracked that time for a few people, I've been told. It definitely did for me. In those weird times of being shut away, I think it offered some kind of solace. So I feel really proud of that one.

Lauren: I was chatting to the founders of Melbourne Electronic Sound Studio, MESS. I don't know if you're familiar with their work, but they've got this massive collection of rare synthesisers that you can play, and Alessandro visited when he was here last time. Apparently he was very hard to impress, because he already had most of them in his own studio. But they've got a VCS1, of which only three were ever made, and apparently Alessandro went a bit quiet when he saw that one.

Daniel: I bet.

Lauren: Are you into synths? Are you a bit of a gearhead?

Daniel: Not as much as those guys. I really like old machines, but I also really like modern techniques, and I use a lot of stuff within the laptop. At the same time, I really like live instrumentation as well. I always have, but I've pushed that forward on the new record. I like the spaces where all of those things intersect. I don't feel like a purist in any way. I like using everything I have in front of me.

Lauren: Your studio sounds pretty amazing too. Is it still in that shipping container by the river Thames in London?

Daniel: I've been there since the beginning, really. I've been there since 2012.

Lauren: It sounds like a pretty special space for you. Can you describe it? You do a lot of recordings of the atmosphere around there too, don't you?

Daniel: Yeah, that's correct. The space is only tiny. It's a shipping container, so it's a little metal box. But it's the surrounding area that's important to me. You're right in the middle of London, but you're also by the water. It feels really serene and quiet, and it's not the easiest spot to get to, which I really like. It's tucked away in this little corner, surrounded by other great musicians and artists, and there's an illustration school down there, and a dance school. It's this weird little special corner of London that I feel so lucky to be a part of. I always say that I think the sound of my music is often trying to find the space between the madness of the nightclub and the road, and the quiet times away from it. And I think the marriage of those two is what influences so much of what I do.

Lauren: You've also spoken a lot about the warmth of distortion, and almost wanting to set things on fire, not literally, and about the transcendental beauty of noise. What kind of emotions were you chasing on this new record?

Daniel: I've always loved heavy music in lots of forms, and I've always found it really comforting and warm and inviting. I don't know, it must just be how my brain is wired, because I feel the same way about a lot of — I like quite dark films, and I find a certain comfort in them. I was always drawn to the more shadowy end of everything, really: films, books, music. I don't know why exactly, but when it comes to music, I love the idea of beauty being hidden beneath distortion, or noise surrounding a really strong hook. I just really love it. I find it warm and inviting.

Lauren: You've talked about the listening phase of an album, and how listening while you're moving can be a totally different experience. Do you absorb music differently when you're listening and moving at the same time?

Daniel: I think it's my favourite way to do it, actually. I guess just because I'm travelling so much, but it must have something to do with this idea of companionship: you're never alone when you have music. I've always really loved that idea. I'm often on my own travelling, physically, but if I have a record in my ears, in my mind, then it's a different experience, and that can be really heavy, enveloping music. I really enjoy that when I'm listening to other records. And it's often the final test of my own stuff: travelling with it.

Lauren: Earlier in your career, you were taken under the wing of mentors like Erol Alkan, and of course the late, great Andrew Weatherall, both renowned for bridging the worlds of rock and dance music. Only if you feel comfortable, I'd love to talk about your relationship with Andrew Weatherall. You put out that tribute track for him. How would you describe his legacy, and what did he teach you?

Daniel: Well, there are a few things to say here. From afar, before I ever met him, much like Erol, I was really drawn to him because I could tell he didn't come from your standard electronic music background. He came from a more left-field spot, and he definitely wasn't interested in being a superstar DJ. When I was growing up in the late nineties, that whole world seemed pretty gross to me, and I wasn't interested. So when I discovered figures like Andrew, I just thought, oh, maybe I could have a spot in this world. It was really inviting. And when I met him, all the things I wanted to be true were true. He was just genuine, and wanted to support new stuff. He never stopped moving. You couldn't take your eyes off him, because there was a new project of some variety seemingly every six months: a new record, a new club night, a new idea he was putting out into the world. And he was just genuine. I'm going to keep coming back to that word.

It's important for me to say that he never would have wanted to call himself a mentor. Definitely not. He would have been far too humble for that. But what I gleaned from him was that you can't go wrong if you just are yourself, and that's really the only goal. One thing he would talk about is that trends come and go all the time, and to follow them is just a fool's game, really. So if you can just be yourself, and do something that feels true to you, then you can't — it's actually impossible to put a foot wrong. You might be more popular one day than the next, but you're going to leave something behind that you're proud of. And there's no greater example to me than Andrew Weatherall.

Lauren: What was the decision behind making a full remix album? Were there other remix records that inspired you?

Daniel: Yeah, there were. I really like it when an artist takes their own work and recontextualises it. I think the Human League kind of came up with the concept, I guess; it's definitely an early one, 82, I think. The Cure's Mixed Up is a big one for me. Nine Inch Nails have done several over the years. I loved Massive Attack vs. Mad Professor. And Soulwax's Nite Versions was a huge one for me as a teenager, where they took their own rock record and turned it into something more techno-leaning. That was an enormous record for me. All of those things, really. There was never a plan to make a club version of the album, but I did a couple, and I enjoyed it so much that I just did the whole thing, and it came together really naturally. I'm really happy with it. It feels like two sides of the same coin for me.

Lauren: Speaking of influences, are you excited about the new Boards of Canada record on the way? Were they a big one for you?

Daniel: Absolutely. All of that Warp stuff. Autechre as well. And obviously Aphex. Again, just oddball music that sounds kind of alien, but full of this humanity, really, and hooks and melodies. And they've managed to create these worlds you can just get lost inside. So, in short, yeah, I am really excited.

Lauren: We're really excited that you're bringing your live show to Australia. What can audiences expect?

Daniel: I would like to think that if you have enjoyed any corner of my music, there'll be something for you in the live show. But it's not a DJ set. There are rave elements to it, huge techno elements, so if you like that side of what I do, you'll definitely find something. But it also touches on the guitar-led side of what I do. It's a really intense experience. There are serene moments, and there are very loud moments. It's a real short, sharp shock: the intensity of a rock show, but with the heartbeat of a techno rave. That's probably a more concise way of saying it.

Lauren: Looking forward to you turning Melbourne Town Hall into a big rave room. Thanks heaps for chatting to me today, Daniel.

Daniel: Thank you so much. It's been great.
